visual.left_sub: the first facts blurred by time and distance
visual.right: A confession from the first years
visual.question: How early does the belief go?

say: The standard skeptical move against the resurrection has long been to treat it as legend — a story that grew by accretion over decades, the original facts blurred by time and distance.
So the real question is whether the belief is early enough to rule out legend.
And the answer is hidden inside a letter the apostle Paul wrote to a church in Corinth around the year 55.

scenes.kicker: A TRADITION OLDER THAN THE LETTER

visual.text: “… that Christ died for our sins, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.”

say: In that letter, Paul pauses to remind his readers of something he insists he did not invent.

“For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received,” he writes: that Christ died for our sins, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
The arresting thing is not the content alone but the framing: Paul is quoting.
He uses the technical language of rabbinic tradition — receiving and delivering a fixed body of teaching — reciting a formula older than the letter that contains it.

scenes.kicker: THE MARKS OF A BORROWED FORMULA

items.label: MARK 2 · NOT PAUL’S OWN WORDING
items.text: “for our sins,” “the twelve,” “according to the Scriptures”

items.label: MARK 3 · BUILT TO RECITE
items.text: Balanced, fourfold lines: died · buried · raised · appeared

say: Several converging features show he is handing on a borrowed formula.
First, the verbs: Paul “delivered” what he “received” — the precise idiom Judaism used for passing on authoritative tradition.
Second, the wording is in part not Paul’s own — “for our sins,” “the twelve,” “according to the Scriptures” cluster non-Pauline vocabulary into a few lines.
Third, the structure is liturgical: balanced lines in a fourfold rhythm — died, buried, raised, appeared — a confession built to be memorized, not prose composed on the fly.

window.label: the creed already formed — within ~2–5 years of the cross

say: If the creed is older than the letter, how much older? The argument runs through Paul’s own biography.
Most historians place the crucifixion around AD 30 to 33.
Paul’s conversion follows within a year or three of it.
Then, he says, after three years he went up to Jerusalem, met Cephas, and also saw James the Lord’s brother — a visit that falls around AD 36 to 38.
And those two men are precisely two of the named witnesses in the creed.

The letter to Corinth itself comes later, around the year 55 — but the tradition must predate Paul’s receiving it: no later than the mid-to-late 30s, and, if he already had it at his conversion, within roughly two to five years of the cross.
This is not a conclusion driven by apologetic motive; it is held across the spectrum — the atheist New Testament scholar Gerd Lüdemann dated its elements “not later than three years.”

scenes.kicker: WHAT IT PROVES — AND WHAT IT DOESN’T
say: The payoff is significant — and so is the limit.

The creed shows that the four-part claim — died, buried, raised, appeared — was the bedrock confession of the movement from its earliest traceable moment, naming as its witnesses the movement’s own leaders: Peter, James, and the twelve.
The window is too narrow for legend to have done its slow work, and the named witnesses were still alive and widely known.
But here intellectual honesty demands a hard line.
The creed establishes early, sincere, eyewitness-anchored belief in Jesus’ death, burial, and appearances; it does not, by itself, prove the resurrection.
That their conviction was true is a further inference, argued on separate grounds — the empty tomb, the failure of the alternatives, the conversion of skeptics like James and Paul.

visual.claim: “It was visions, and nothing else” — grief-driven experiences, retold until the tradition spoke of mass appearances.

points.t: Hallucinations are private — the creed reports group appearances
James and Paul were hostile: no grief to trigger a vision
And it leaves the empty tomb unaddressed

say: The most prominent skeptical voice here, Bart Ehrman, grants a great deal: he affirms that the disciples came to believe they had seen Jesus alive.
But his explanation is naturalistic — “it was visions, and nothing else,” akin to the well-documented bereavement visions in which the grieving perceive a lost loved one.
One should concede the point: the bare report “they saw him” is, on its face, compatible with hallucination.
The reply turns on the details the vision hypothesis has to explain away.
Hallucinations are, as a rule, private and individual — yet the creed reports group appearances, to “the twelve” and to “more than five hundred.”
It must also account for two men who had no grief to trigger a vision: James, a skeptic, and Paul, an active persecutor.
On the full set of facts — the group appearances, the hostile-witness conversions, the empty tomb — the vision hypothesis is left wanting.

scenes.kicker: ONE STRAND OF A STRONGER CASE

visual.dest: → the first premise, not the whole case

say: So the creed is the indispensable first premise of the resurrection case, not the whole of it.
It hands the deeper question — what best explains their experiences and the empty tomb — to the wider argument.
The empty tomb, the failure of every alternative, the conversions of James and Paul — together these carry the weight the creed alone cannot.

visual.text: “This tradition, we can be entirely confident, was formulated as tradition within months of Jesus’ death.”
visual.cite: James D. G. Dunn, Jesus Remembered (2003), 855

say: The early date of the creed is about as close to a consensus as ancient history offers.
On the creed’s early date, Jeremias, Conzelmann, Wright, Lüdemann, and Ehrman — believers and atheists alike — agree.
The British critical historian James D. G. Dunn, no apologist, put the lower bound most memorably.

head: A borrowed creed —
older than the Gospels.
visual.sub: Early. Sincere. From named witnesses. The right place for any serious inquiry to begin.

say: The creed of 1 Corinthians 15 establishes, with a confidence rare in the study of antiquity, that within a few years of the cross the earliest Christians were already confessing Jesus’ death, burial, resurrection, and appearances.
It does not, on its own, prove that Jesus rose; it proves the belief is early and the witnesses sincere, and hands the deeper question to the wider case.
And this is what we hold to be true: Jesus of Nazareth was bodily raised from the dead, as this creed confesses.
The case is to be made, as Peter urged, with gentleness and respect — confident in what the evidence shows, candid about where it ends.
